translation: (Voiceover): O cuckoo, black cuckoo, my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo; O cuckoo, black cuckoo, my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo; my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo

Pallavi: The mouth that ate neem turned sweet, but the belly turned bitter, cuckoo; the belly turned bitter, cuckoo; the belly turned bitter, cuckoo; carrying loads, your head grew light, but life grew heavy, cuckoo; life grew heavy, cuckoo; life grew heavy, cuckoo; baked in the sun, cuckoo, you became a dark shade, cuckoo; baked in the sun, cuckoo, you became a dark shade, cuckoo; flowing out as sweat, cuckoo, you became the village tanks, cuckoo; flowing out as sweat, cuckoo, you became the village tanks, cuckoo; you carried the whole village, so how did you become the burden? Don't stay silent, mother cuckoo; O cuckoo, black cuckoo, my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo; my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo

Verse 1: Rising in the small hours, she became the moon, the cuckoo who does the scrubbing chores; the cuckoo who does the scrubbing chores; the cuckoo who does the scrubbing chores; her body worn to pieces, the whole house gleamed, a creature with only her own wings, cuckoo; a creature with only her own wings, cuckoo; a creature with only her own wings, cuckoo; the mother who bore and raised them, cuckoo, yet the children are not counted as yours, cuckoo; the mother who bore and raised them, cuckoo, yet the children are not counted as yours, cuckoo; in your in-laws' house, cuckoo, you are the harvest of the ones who bore you, cuckoo; in your in-laws' house, cuckoo, you are the harvest of the ones who bore you, cuckoo; belonging neither there nor here, ask how a woman's life came to be this way, my mother cuckoo; O cuckoo, black cuckoo, my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo; my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo

Verse 2: When you bent your back the seedlings were planted; you are a crop among the crops, cuckoo, you; a crop among the crops, cuckoo, you; a crop among the crops, cuckoo; when you took up basket and shovel, houses became mansions; you are a brick among the bricks, cuckoo, you; a brick among the bricks, cuckoo, you; a brick among the bricks, cuckoo; cuckoo who dug the wells, cuckoo who built so many bungalows; cuckoo who dug the wells, cuckoo who built so many bungalows; calling you a 'woman labourer', cuckoo, they paid you differently, cuckoo; calling you a 'woman labourer', cuckoo, they paid you differently, cuckoo; how can work and wages differ for women and men? Ask it, cuckoo, you who do every kind of work; O cuckoo, black cuckoo, my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo; my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo

Verse 3: You are the family goddess who gives birth to the clan, yet your caste, it seems, is the male caste, cuckoo; your caste, it seems, is the male caste, cuckoo; your caste, it seems, is the male caste, cuckoo; if castes are mixed, you are left with ostracism and climb onto the sacrificial altar, cuckoo; you climb onto the sacrificial altar, cuckoo; you climb onto the sacrificial altar, cuckoo; what caste does reaping have, cuckoo? What caste does carrying paddy have, cuckoo? What caste does reaping have, cuckoo? What caste does carrying paddy have, cuckoo? What caste does water have, cuckoo? Hey, what caste does fire have, cuckoo? What caste does water have, cuckoo? Hey, what caste does fire have, cuckoo? Am I a pot for the whole village, a doll in the marketplace? Cuckoo who defies the laws of caste; O cuckoo, black cuckoo, my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo; my dark mother, cuckoo, mother of us Shudra folk, cuckoo

Verse 4: Demand the right to plough, cuckoo, demand your share in the fields, cuckoo; demand your share in the fields, cuckoo; demand your share in the fields, cuckoo; stop the drudgery of housework, cuckoo, demand the fruit of your labour, cuckoo; demand the fruit of your labour, cuckoo; demand the fruit of your labour, cuckoo; not just bearing and raising children, cuckoo, hey, demand your inheritance, cuckoo; not just bearing and raising children, cuckoo, hey, demand your inheritance, cuckoo; don't become a prisoner of looks and beauty, cuckoo; don't become a prisoner of looks and beauty, cuckoo; all these rights, I claim them, cuckoo, and you raise your iron fist, cuckoo; all these rights, I claim them, cuckoo, and you raise your iron fist, cuckoo; all these rights, I claim them, cuckoo, and you raise your iron fist, cuckoo; all these rights, I claim them, cuckoo, and you raise your iron fist, cuckoo
summaryEn: Koyila Nalla Koyila ('O Cuckoo, Black Cuckoo') is sung by Vimalakka on the album Vimalakka Hits (2023). In this song of women's rights, the singer addresses the koel, the black cuckoo, as 'my dark mother' and the mother of the Shudra (labouring-caste) folk. The bird stands for the working woman, dark from the sun and unseen, yet sustaining everything. The chorus uses striking reversals. Her mouth turned sweet from eating neem while her belly turned bitter; her head grew light from carrying loads while life grew heavy; her sweat filled the village tanks. The verses trace her unpaid and underpaid labour: scrubbing before dawn, no claim on the children she raises, an outsider in her in-laws' house, planting, carrying bricks, digging wells, and still earning less as a 'woman labourer'. The third verse attacks caste and patriarchy together: a woman's caste is decided by men, a mixed-caste marriage can lead to ostracism or death, and yet reaping, water and fire have no caste. The last verse turns into a list of demands: the right to plough, a share of the land, an end to housework drudgery, inheritance, and freedom from being judged by beauty. It ends with a call to raise an iron fist. Nearly every phrase ends in 'koyila' and repeats, giving a chant-like pull.
summaryTe: ‘కోయిల నల్ల కోయిల’ విమలక్క 2023 ‘విమలక్క హిట్స్’ ఆల్బమ్‌లో పాడిన పాట. ఇది కులాన్ని కూడా ప్రశ్నించే స్త్రీ హక్కుల గీతం. గాయని నల్లని కోయిలను ‘నల్లని నా తల్లి’గా, ‘సుద్దరోళ్ళ అవ్వ’గా - అంటే శ్రమజీవుల తల్లిగా - సంబోధిస్తుంది. ఎండకు నల్లబడ్డ, ఎవరికీ కనిపించని, అయినా అన్నిటినీ మోసే శ్రామిక స్త్రీకి ఆ పక్షి ప్రతీక. పల్లవిలో తలకిందుల ఉపమానాలు గుండెను తాకుతాయి: యాప తిన్న నోరు తీపైతే కడుపు చేదైంది; బరువు మోసి నెత్తి అలుకైతే బతుకు బరువైంది; ఆమె చెమటే పల్లె చెరువులైంది. చరణాలు ఆమె శ్రమను వివరిస్తాయి - జాము రాతిరే లేచి పాచి పనులు, కనిపెంచిన బిడ్డలపై హక్కు లేకపోవడం, అత్తింట్లో పరాయిదానిగా బతకడం, నాట్లు వేయడం, ఇటుకలు మోయడం, బావులు తవ్వడం, బంగ్లాలు కట్టడం; అయినా ‘ఆడకూలి’ అని తక్కువ కూలి. మూడో చరణం కులాన్ని, పితృస్వామ్యాన్ని కలిపి ప్రశ్నిస్తుంది: స్త్రీ కులాన్ని మగవాళ్ళే నిర్ణయిస్తారు; కులాంతర ప్రేమకు వెలివేత, బలిపీఠం మిగులుతాయి; కానీ కోతకు, నీళ్ళకు, నిప్పుకు కులం ఏది? చివరి చరణం డిమాండ్ల జాబితాగా మారుతుంది - దున్నే హక్కు, భూమిలో వాటా, ఇంటి చాకిరి నుంచి విముక్తి, వారసత్వ హక్కు, అందచందాల బందిఖానా నుంచి విడుదల - ఉక్కు పిడికిలి ఎత్తమనే పిలుపుతో ముగుస్తుంది. దాదాపు ప్రతి పదబంధం ‘కోయిలా’తో ముగిసి మళ్ళీ మళ్ళీ రావడం పాటకు వెంటాడే లయను ఇస్తుంది.
